procedural_history.originating_court: Trial Court (convicted the appellants under Sections 323, 324 and 325 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.12.2023 of the High Court of M.P. Principal Seat at Jabalpur in CRLA No. 1999 of 2013
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Madhya Pradesh High Court disposed of the criminal appeal of the appellants by maintaining their conviction and sentence as awarded by the Trial Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants appealed to the Supreme Court, which invoked its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution and set aside the conviction of the appellants.

directions: Appellants, who are already outside jail, need not surrender.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction for a non-compoundable offence under Section 324 of the IPC can be set aside by invoking powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, based on a settlement between the parties who are close relatives.

facts: The appellants were convicted under Sections 323, 324, and 325 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) following an incident with their relatives.
The incident arose from a minor dispute over the appellants objecting to the respondents tying bullocks on land they claimed was theirs.
After conviction, the parties, who are close relatives (cousins and an uncle), reached a settlement.
As part of the settlement, the appellants tendered an unconditional apology, and the injured respondents agreed to compound the offence and maintain peace.
law: Offences under Sections 323 and 325 of the IPC are compoundable, meaning they can be settled between the parties with the court's permission.
The offence under Section 324 of the IPC is non-compoundable, meaning it cannot ordinarily be settled by the parties once a conviction is recorded.
The Supreme Court has extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice.
This power under Article 142 can be invoked to set aside a conviction for a non-compoundable offence, but only in exceptional cases.
The Court considers several factors before invoking this power, including the relationship between the parties, the nature of the incident, and the impact of the crime on society.
application: The Court acknowledged that the conviction under Section 324 IPC was for a non-compoundable offence.
However, it identified this as an exceptional case suitable for the use of its extraordinary powers.
The Court noted that the parties were close relatives, and the dispute was of a minor nature with no significant impact on society at large.
The Court gave weight to the fact that the parties had voluntarily settled their differences and agreed to live in peace and harmony.
Considering these specific circumstances, the Court concluded that this was a "fit case" to invoke its powers under Article 142 to prioritize the settlement and familial harmony over the conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court invoked its extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution and set aside the appellants' conviction for the non-compoundable offence under Section 324 of the IPC, based on the settlement reached between the parties who were close relatives.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction for a non-compoundable offence under Section 324 of the IPC can be set aside by invoking powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, based on a settlement between the parties who are close relatives.
appellant_arguments: The appellants have settled the dispute with the injured persons, who are their close relatives (Uncle and Nephew).
A formal Compromise Deed dated 29.01.2024 has been executed to this effect with the intervention of family elders.
The appellants prayed for the court's permission to compound the offence based on the amicable settlement.
respondent_arguments: The injured persons, impleaded as private respondents, filed affidavits confirming that they have agreed to compound the offence.
The agreement to compound the offence is based on the fact that the parties are close relatives (cousins and uncle-nephew) and the appellants have tendered an unconditional apology.
The dispute has been settled amicably with the intervention of family elders, and the compromise is voluntary.

cases.case_name: Ramgopal & Anr. v. State of M.P
cases.principle: For the principle of invoking powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to set aside a conviction for non-compoundable offenses based on a settlement between the parties.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court may invoke its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to set aside a conviction where the dispute was between close relatives over a minor issue, and the parties have subsequently settled their disputes amicably with an agreement to maintain future peace and harmony.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In our case, the incident occurred on 20.05.2011 relating to a minor issue where respondent no.2 was trying to tie bullocks to which the appellants objected by saying that it was their land. As is clear from the compromise, the appellants and complainant side are close relatives and after settling their disputes, both sides have agreed to maintain peace and harmony in the society. Taking all of this into account, we invoke our powers under Article 142 of the Constitution and hereby, set aside the conviction of appellants in the present case.
legal_tests_applied: Invoking powers under Article 142 to quash criminal proceedings in non-compoundable offences is to be done only in exceptional cases after considering various factors including the nature of injuries, relation between parties and the impact of crime on society.
The court must consider the nature and effect of the offence on the conscience of the society.
policy_considerations: When parties, who are close relatives, have settled their disputes, allowing the conviction to be set aside promotes peace and harmony in the society.
The court should consider the impact of the crime on society and the effect of the offence on the conscience of the society when deciding whether to exercise its extraordinary powers.
